segments.title: Introduction
segments.text: Hi, and welcome to Small Models, Real Systems, the weekly research digest by Mylari. This is edition three, for Wednesday the fourteenth of October, 2026. This week: five picks on what it takes to ship a small model, from the labels it learns from to serving settings nobody looks at. Two of them replace a frontier model outright.

segments.title: Preply - a fine-tuned 0.8B grammar annotator beats frontier models
segments.text: First, Preply, the online tutoring platform. In a paper posted on the seventh of October, they track which grammar concepts English learners use correctly in lesson transcripts. The pilot prompted GPT-5.4 with an almost four-thousand-token prompt, too expensive to roll out. So they fine-tuned a Qwen 3.5 model of just zero point eight billion parameters with LoRA. The training data was teacher annotations that GPT-5.4 re-reviewed and rules validated, plus synthetic examples for rare concepts and errors. That cleanup alone added about forty points of strict recall over raw teacher labels, and the prompt shrank by ninety percent. On human-curated benchmarks the small model beat the prompted frontier models, at about one sixteenth of the serving cost.

segments.title: eBay - generative vs encoder students for topic tagging
segments.text: Second, eBay. Once GPT-4o has labelled your data, which student should you train: an encoder classifier like DeBERTa, or a small generative model that writes the labels out? It depends on the text. On product reviews, DeBERTa beat a one-billion-parameter generator. On multi-turn buyer-seller chats, even the one-billion model won. And as the chat taxonomy grew from ten topics to a hundred and twelve, DeBERTa's macro F1 fell by about a third, while the eight-billion model barely moved. The catch: generators invent labels like shipping-issue, so production maps them back to the taxonomy or drops them. The eight-billion model now serves both uses, and reviews passing the quality bar rose sixty percent in a live test.

segments.title: Consultant - distilling a job-title model to 350M on a CPU
segments.text: Third, an engineering post from Consultant, a contractor job board, published on the tenth. They turn messy multilingual job titles into one clean English title. The biggest win came before training: the model names the role and quotes its evidence, but never picks the seniority. Rules read the level from a verbatim quote, which stopped invented seniority. Then a fine-tuned two-billion Gemma model labelled about twenty thousand postings for a three-hundred-and-fifty-million-parameter student. On two hundred held-out postings from unseen sources, the student matched its teacher at eighty-eight percent. Trained on the original two thousand rows alone, it trailed. More data mattered, not more parameters. It runs on a five-and-a-half-euro-a-month CPU server.

segments.title: Amazon - serving settings change classifier predictions
segments.text: Fourth, a warning for anyone serving classifiers, from Amazon researchers. They trained a hundred and eighty classifiers, then changed only serving settings, with the same checkpoint and the same text. Changing the padded length alone flipped about ten percent of labels, because tokens shifted to new positions. In full precision, changing batch shape flipped no labels. In bfloat16, it moved up to fifty-seven points of probability mass, which thresholds and rankings consume. Generative classifiers flipped more labels than encoders. Their advice: pin the serving settings, and monitor probabilities, not just labels.

segments.title: Enterpret - plausible taxonomies that fail as a whole
segments.text: Fifth, taxonomy quality, from Enterpret, a customer-feedback analytics company. They had an agentic harness generate category trees over two real feedback corpora. Every generated tree passed the usual LLM-judge checks on names, parents and siblings. Yet at least ninety-seven percent of their leaf names just restated an ancestor's name, and in one tree, three of every four records fell under more than one top-level category. Their fix is whole-tree metrics: is the shape learned from the data, and do branches split feedback into groups a team can own. If your small model tags against a taxonomy, test the tree too.

segments.title: Patterns this week and sign-off
segments.text: The pattern this week: the label contract matters as much as the model. Preply and Consultant won with cleaner, checkable outputs. eBay's best student depended on the text. And Amazon and Enterpret show that how you serve and what you measure can quietly change the answer. Links and numbers are in the show notes. Thanks for listening, and see you next Wednesday.
